Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Diplomat
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drug Use: take drugs, Compulsive Exercise: I push myself to exercise excessively, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Hopelessness: I have no future

Vignette:
Arjun Kapoor was twenty-four years old when he sat down in a therapist's office for the first time, still wearing the layered jackets and long sleeves that had become his uniform over the past eighteen months. But the fracture had begun two years earlier, on the morning of March 14th, when he was twenty-two and working as a junior diplomatic aide at the embassy compound in Beirut. He had been in the basement archive sorting visa applications—methodical work that suited his nature, his fluency in Arabic, his careful ambition to build a career in the Foreign Service. His family in New Jersey had celebrated the posting with the kind of pride that made it impossible to fail. When the first mortar round struck the building above, the sound was not like anything he had heard before—not a car backfire or construction blast, but a deep, percussive crack that seemed to originate inside his own chest. The lights went out. In the darkness came a sharp, acrid smell mixed with plaster dust and something else he could not name—alcohol, perhaps, someone's spilled drink, or something ignited by the blast itself. A second explosion followed, closer. He felt the floor move beneath him, felt his hands scrape raw against concrete as he was pulled toward the stairs by a security officer, his ears ringing, his mind fragmenting. Three people died in the compound that day. Arjun was not among them.

He spent two days in a Lebanese hospital and was evacuated within forty-eight hours, released with minor lacerations and a diagnosis of acute stress reaction. By April, he was back in Washington at a different desk in the State Department building, telling himself and everyone around him—his girlfriend Priya, his supervisor, his parents—that he was fortunate, that the posting was simply over, that he should move forward. The reassurances felt true enough in daylight. But by autumn, something had shifted in ways he could not articulate. He found himself checking the locks on his apartment door multiple times each night, a ritual that sometimes stretched until three or four in the morning, his hands trembling as he turned the deadbolt again and again, each check failing to produce the certainty he needed. At the State Department, he sat with his back to the wall in every meeting, studying colleagues' hands and posture, the angle at which they approached him. Even in the secure corridors surrounded by other diplomats and security personnel, he carried an absolute conviction that he was in danger—not the abstract kind, but the imminent, specific kind that made his skin feel too tight. When colleagues would reassure him, "You're safe here, Arjun, you're home," he would nod, but the reassurance never penetrated the part of him that remained certain something catastrophic was about to happen. The smell of alcohol became intolerable. At a departmental reception in November, someone spilled wine near him, and the acrid burning smell from that morning in Beirut flooded his senses so completely that he left the building without explanation. Priya found him in the parking garage, breathing heavily, unable to articulate why he had fled.

His memories of the explosion were vivid and intrusive—he could see the ceiling tiles falling, could feel the pressure in his ears, could smell that confusing mixture of alcohol and destruction—yet when he tried to tell Priya what he was experiencing, the words dissolved into nothing. He knew what had happened. He had been there. But the specifics seemed to exist in a language he no longer spoke. He began running obsessively, sometimes for two hours at a time, pushing through pain in his legs and chest as though exhaustion might outrun the thoughts that chased him. He started wearing the loose, layered clothing because being visible, being noticed by people on the street, made his skin crawl. A stranger approaching him on the Metro would trigger a surge of panic so intense that he would move cars or get off at the next stop. He had lost weight. Priya asked if he was using again—he had smoked marijuana occasionally in college—and he had lied and said no. In truth, he had started buying it regularly, using it most evenings to quiet the noise in his head, and had begun experimenting with other things: pills he could obtain through friends, anything that would create distance between himself and the certainty that something terrible was about to happen. By January, his work performance had declined noticeably. His supervisor noted that he seemed withdrawn in meetings, that he had missed a briefing without explanation. He had been passed over for a promotion he had expected. Priya had begun to withdraw as well, exhausted by his unavailability and his refusal to explain what was happening. She had asked him directly, three weeks ago, whether he still wanted to be in the relationship. He had not answered because he was not sure.

He had come to believe that something fundamental in him—some flaw, some weakness—had made him the kind of person who would be in that basement when the building came down. Others had survived; others had gone on to their lives intact. But Arjun carried the sense that the event had selected him specifically, had exposed something true about him that he could not articulate and could not escape. The conviction that he was fundamentally unsafe, that danger adhered to him in ways that others could sense, had become the organizing principle of his existence. It was Priya's ultimatum that finally moved him to call the Veterans Affairs crisis line three weeks ago. He had no right to that resource—he was a civilian, not a soldier—but the counselor who answered did not turn him away. Within a week, he was sitting in a therapist's office, still wearing his concealing layers, still unable to find words for what he needed to say, but finally willing to try. What frightened him most was not the memories themselves, vivid as they were, but the possibility that they would never fade—that he would spend the rest of his life in that basement, checking locks, studying strangers' hands, waiting for the next explosion.
